Q: What is a Thread in Java?
Ans
• A thread is a lightweight subprocess, the smallest unit of processing. Multithreading allows concurrent execution of two or more parts of a program.

Q: What is the role of the JVM?
Ans
• JVM acts as a run-time engine to run Java applications. It loads, verifies, and executes code while providing a runtime environment.

Q: What are the four pillars of OOPs?
Ans
• The four pillars are Inheritance, Polymorphism, Encapsulation, and Abstraction.

Q: Difference between String and StringBuilder?
Ans
• String is immutable (cannot be changed), whereas StringBuilder is mutable and more efficient for frequent modifications.

Q: Interface vs Abstract Class?
Ans
• Interfaces support multiple inheritance and have only abstract methods (pre-Java 8), while abstract classes can have constructors and concrete methods.

Q: What is Exception Handling?
Ans
• It is a mechanism to handle runtime errors using try, catch, finally, throw, and throws keywords to maintain normal application flow.

Q: What is the Difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
Ans • JDK is the development kit containing JRE and tools; JRE provides the libraries to run applications, and JVM is the engine that actually executes the bytecode.

Q: What is the purpose of the 'static' keyword?
Ans • The static keyword means the variable or method belongs to the class itself rather than an instance, allowing it to be accessed without creating an object.

Q: What is a Constructor in Java?
Ans • A constructor is a special method used to initialize objects; it has the same name as the class and no explicit return type.

Q: What is the 'final' keyword used for?
Ans • The final keyword is used to restrict the user: a final variable cannot be changed, a final method cannot be overridden, and a final class cannot be inherited.

Q: What is the difference between Array and ArrayList?
Ans • An Array is fixed in size, while an ArrayList is a dynamic collection that grows and shrinks automatically as elements are added or removed.

Q: What is Method Overloading vs Overriding?
Ans • Overloading happens when multiple methods have the same name but different parameters within the same class; Overriding occurs when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its parent class.

Today is Friday, March 27, 2026. Let's dive into the Core Java essentials for your technical review.

1. Why is Java popular?

Java's 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA) capability, robust security, automatic memory management (GC), and huge community support make it a top choice for enterprise apps.
code:
// Java runs on any device with a JVM
System.out.println("Hello World from any OS!");

body:
2. Why is Java not 100% Object-Oriented?

Java is not purely object-oriented because it supports primitive data types (int, char, boolean, etc.) that are not objects. However, wrapper classes help bridge this gap.
code:
int x = 10; // Primitive (Not an object)
Integer y = Integer.valueOf(10); // Object version

body:
3. What is the 'static' keyword?

The static keyword means the member belongs to the class itself rather than to individual instances. It helps in memory management by sharing a single copy across all objects.

4. Abstract Class vs Interface

Abstract Class: Can have constructors and both abstract/concrete methods. Interface: Primarily defines a contract. Since Java 8, it can have default/static methods.
code:
interface Drawable { void draw(); }
abstract class Shape { abstract void area(); }

body:
5. final, finally, and finalize

final: Constant/Non-inheritable. finally: A block that always executes after try-catch. finalize: A method called by the GC before destroying an object (deprecated).
code:
final int MAX = 100;
try { } finally { System.out.println("Always runs"); }

body:
6. Why are Strings Immutable?

Security, Synchronization, and the String Constant Pool. If multiple variables point to the same string, changing one shouldn't affect the others.

7. String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer

String: Immutable. StringBuilder: Mutable and fast (not thread-safe). StringBuffer: Mutable and thread-safe (synchronized/slower).
code:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
sb.append(" Syed"); // Modifies the same object

body:
8. Wrapper Classes & Autoboxing

Wrapper classes convert primitives into objects. Autoboxing is the automatic conversion the Java compiler makes between primitives and their corresponding wrapper classes.
code:
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(5); // Autoboxing: int 5 to Integer

body:
9. Access Modifiers in Java

Private: Class only. Default: Package only. Protected: Package + Subclasses. Public: Visible everywhere.
code:
private String secret;
public String name;

body:
10. Overloading vs Overriding

Overloading: Same method name, different parameters (Compile-time). Overriding: Redefining a parent method in a child class (Run-time).
code:
// Overloading: add(int, int), add(double, double)
// Overriding: @Override public void run() { ... }

body:
11. 'this' vs 'super' Keywords

this: Refers to the current class instance. super: Refers to the immediate parent class instance or constructor.
code:
this.name = name; // current class variable
super.eat();     // calls parent method

body:
12. Exception Hierarchy (Checked vs Unchecked)

Checked: Handled at compile-time (IOException). Unchecked: Occur at runtime (NullPointerException/ArithmeticException).

13. Object Class Methods

Every class in Java inherits from the Object class. Key methods include: toString(), equals(), hashCode(), clone(), and getClass().

14. Java Memory: Stack vs Heap

Stack: Stores local variables and method execution frames. Heap: Stores all objects created using the 'new' keyword. Garbage collection happens in the Heap.
code:
Person p = new Person();
// 'p' is on Stack, actual Person object on Heap

body:
15. Constructor Overloading

Having multiple constructors with the same name but different parameter lists. It allows initializing objects in different ways.
